Chapter Four: The Discovery of Hepatitis B

In the decades that followed the Second World War, public health officials across Europe and North America watched a quiet epidemic unfold. Blood transfusion, then a routine and often life-saving procedure, carried risks that few clinicians understood. Patients who received donated plasma sometimes developed jaundice weeks later, and the cause remained obscure. Researchers suspected an infectious agent, but conventional culture techniques failed again and again. The search would occupy a generation of virologists and change the way laboratories handled human blood.

The first breakthrough came through a study of serum proteins in populations from Australia and Africa. Baruch Blumberg and his colleagues were investigating inherited variation, not infectious disease. Their identification of what became known as the Australia antigen was, in large part, an accident of careful record keeping. Only years later did the antigen's association with post-transfusion hepatitis become clear. The finding turned a narrow biochemical question into one of the most urgent problems in medicine.

Laboratories soon developed sensitive assays, and screening programs followed. Donated blood could be tested before transfusion, and the incidence of transfusion-associated hepatitis fell sharply. Yet the virus itself remained invisible. Electron microscopy revealed spherical particles of remarkable uniformity, and their structure offered few clues about replication. Researchers argued about whether the particles were complete virions or merely fragments of a larger agent.

Progress required new tools. Restriction enzymes, cloning vectors, and eventually automated sequencing allowed laboratories to read viral genomes directly. The first complete sequences of hepatitis B virus were published in the late nineteen seventies, and comparisons between isolates from different continents followed quickly. The genomes were small, circular, and partly double-stranded, an arrangement that puzzled everyone who expected a conventional DNA virus.

As sequencing improved, comparative studies placed the agent within a family of related viruses found in birds and mammals. The family was named Hepadnaviridae, a term combining hepatotropism with a reference to the DNA genome. Members of this group share a distinctive replication strategy involving reverse transcription, an unexpected feature for a virus whose genetic material is DNA. The discovery forced a revision of textbook schemes that separated retroviruses from everything else.

Public health responses developed alongside the basic science. Screening of blood donors, universal vaccination of infants, and antiviral therapy each reduced the burden of disease. In wealthy countries the number of new infections fell dramatically, although the virus remained common in many other regions. Elimination programs depended on reliable supply chains, stable funding, and trust between communities and clinics.

The historical record of this work is scattered across university archives, hospital libraries, and the personal papers of researchers who have since died. One collection, assembled by a virologist who worked on the Australia antigen for more than thirty years, includes laboratory notebooks, correspondence, and thousands of photographic negatives. The archive itself was closed to the public in 1987, and its holdings were transferred to a university repository. Scholars who wish to consult the original notebooks must obtain special permission and travel to the reading room in person.

Reading those notebooks, one is struck by how much of the discovery depended on patience and accident. A sample that should have been discarded was kept; a comparison that seemed irrelevant was pursued. The story resists tidy narratives about heroic individuals. It is a record of institutions, rivalries, and slow accumulation of evidence, and it continues to shape the way scientists think about viruses that hide in plain sight.
